title: Landing gigs and the collapse of the record business
summary: Since moving to New York in 1986, publicity and leadership have become harder, and CD sales are way down and the field cheapened.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: How the music business changed: hype, youth and lost apprenticeship

blocks.x: Does — you moved to New York in the late 80’s?
Okay. Have things gotten more difficult as far as your day-to-day, week-to-week landing gigs?

Well you know the way it is now the whole thing has changed. Now you have to go through yourself, you have to take care of your own publicity, and that’s really hard for me to do that. I’d much rather just go out and work, but I got to the point now where I really have to be a leader sometimes. And that’s a hard thing for me. I really just sit home and practice and work on music, and think about music, and then enjoy life too. So it’s a lot for me to handle. I’m doing the best I can. I’m staying busy and it’s okay so far. But yeah, it is a lot harder.
It’s like the whole other side of being a musician or an artist, like now there’s the business too.

Yeah, there’s the business and because you know it’s 2010 and the actual record business, which is CD’s or MP3’s it’s so weak. The percentage of sales is way down from even ten years ago. It might be down 80 percent. It’s almost a fold. And so that makes it very hard. You know I can put out a CD with some really great musicians and a kid out of college can make a CD with friends and get the same packaging and put it in © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -5-

the stores and it looks just like mine. And not that I’m putting somebody like that down, I’m just saying that when I started recording it was a special thing. You worked for a company. And even though companies in some ways took more money than they should have from the musicians and discriminated sometimes and did some things, in some ways I think that environment was better than what is happening now.
At least there was a company.
Well at least there was a pecking order. You know there was a pecking order. You had to wait your turn. Now it’s like you want to make a CD?
Yeah. You don’t even have to leave your house.

You don’t have to leave your house. Sometimes the level, the level. It doesn’t matter what the level is, it’s about having a CD. And I’m looking for the right word. I guess it’s just cheapens everything. It cheapens the whole industry.
